items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's recall some of the asymptotic notations we've seen in previous lessons, defined in the context of algorithmic complexity.

Content:
The set [MATH: O(g(n))] contains all nonnegative functions [MATH: f(n)] such that [MATH: f(n) \leq c g(n)] for [MATH: c > 0] and sufficiently large [MATH: n.] Formally:
[MATH: O(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq f(n) \leq c g(n) \big\}]
If [MATH: f\in O(g(n)),] then [MATH: c g(n)] is an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH: f,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2f948c5b2ef93d491f29e7ae46268473]

Content:
The set [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] contains all nonnegative functions [MATH: f(n)] such that [MATH: f(n) \geq c g(n)] for [MATH: c > 0] and sufficiently large [MATH: n.] Formally:
[MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n) \leq f(n) \big\}]
If [MATH: f\in \Omega(g(n)),] then [MATH: c g(n)] is an asymptotic lower bound of [MATH: f,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3014ef545bc133c22947a6f6afb9d0d5]

Content:
A related valuable concept for classifying the asymptotic behavior of algorithms is big-theta notation.

Content:
Suppose we have two nonnegative functions [MATH: f(n)] and [MATH: g(n)] such that there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] such that, for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have
[MATH: c_1 g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_2 g(n)]

Content:
as depicted in the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e5490c9a928d23acb3279bc5e0bcc1a8]

Content:
In plain English, beyond some threshold value [MATH: n_0,] the function [MATH: f(n)] is sandwiched between two multiples of [MATH: g(n),] ensuring that [MATH: f(n)] grows at the same rate as [MATH: g(n)] up to constant factors. In such cases, we write
[MATH: f(n) \in \Theta(g(n))]
where the formal definition of the set [MATH: \Theta(g(n))] is given below:
[MATH: \Theta(g(n)) = \left\{ f(n) : \exists c_1 c_2,n_0 \gt 0, \forall n \geq n_0, 0 \leq c_1g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_2 g(n)\right\}]

Content:
Big-Theta notation is helpful because it provides a tight bound on a function's growth by specifying both an upper and a lower bound.

sections.normalized_html: Suppose [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}.] In the context of algorithmic complexity, what is the definition of [MATH: \Theta(n^{10})?]
sections.readable_text: Suppose [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}.] In the context of algorithmic complexity, what is the definition of [MATH: \Theta(n^{10})?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Theta(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1,] [MATH: c_2,] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] lies between [MATH: c_1 \cdot g(n)] and [MATH: c_2 \cdot g(n).]

[MATH: \Theta(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c_1,c_2, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0\leq c_1\cdot g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_2\cdot g(n) \big\}]

Geometrically, this means the following:

The set [MATH: \Theta(n^{10})] consists of all the functions [MATH: f(n),] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1, c_2,] and [MATH: n_0] such that the graph of [MATH: f(n)] lies between [MATH: y=c_1\cdot n^{10}] and [MATH: y=c_2\cdot n^{10}] for all [MATH: n\geq n_0.]

sections.normalized_html: Prove that [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2)] for [MATH: n\in\mathbb N.]
sections.readable_text: Prove that [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2)] for [MATH: n\in\mathbb N.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Theta(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1], [MATH: c_2] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] lies between [MATH: c_1 \cdot g(n)] and [MATH: c_2 \cdot g(n)]

[MATH: \Theta(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c_1,c_2, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c_1\cdot g(n)\leq f(n) \leq c_2\cdot g(n) \big\}]

So, we start as shown below.

We need to show that there exists constants [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] such that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have [MATH: c_1n^2 \leq 3n^2+1 \leq c_2n^2.]

Now, let's isolate [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] on the inequality.

Dividing both sides of the inequality by [MATH: n^2,] we get follows: [MATH: c_{1}n^{2}|≤ 3n^{2} + 1 ≤ c_{2}n^{2}; (c_{1}n^{2})/(n^{2})|≤ (3n^{2} + 1)/(n^{2}) ≤ (c_{2}n^{2})/(n^{2}); c_{1}|≤ (3n^{2})/(n^{2}) + (1)/(n^{2}) ≤ c_{2}; c_{1}|≤ 3 + (1)/(n^{2}) ≤ c_{2}]

Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n^2} = 1] and [MATH: 3+\dfrac{1}{n^2}=4] if [MATH: n=1.] Also, [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n^2}] monotonically approach [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] That means the minimum possible value of [MATH: \left(3+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)] is [MATH: 3] and the maximum is [MATH: 4.] As a result, [MATH: 3\leq 3+\dfrac{1}{n^2} \leq 4] for all [MATH: n \geq 1,] and we can now pick our constants.

By setting [MATH: n_0=1], [MATH: c_1=3] and [MATH: c_2=4] we make the above inequality hold for any [MATH: n \geq n_0.]

Of course, other choices for the constants [MATH: c_1], [MATH: c_2,] and [MATH: n_0] may do the job, but the important thing is we found at least one such combination.

Therefore, [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2).]

Therefore, [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's recall some of the asymptotic notations we've seen in previous lessons, defined in the context of algorithmic complexity.

Content:
The set [MATH: O(g(n))] contains all nonnegative functions [MATH: f(n)] such that [MATH: f(n) \leq c g(n)] for [MATH: c > 0] and sufficiently large [MATH: n.] Formally:
[MATH: O(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq f(n) \leq c g(n) \big\}]
If [MATH: f\in O(g(n)),] then [MATH: c g(n)] is an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH: f,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2f948c5b2ef93d491f29e7ae46268473]

Content:
The set [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] contains all nonnegative functions [MATH: f(n)] such that [MATH: f(n) \geq c g(n)] for [MATH: c > 0] and sufficiently large [MATH: n.] Formally:
[MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n) \leq f(n) \big\}]
If [MATH: f\in \Omega(g(n)),] then [MATH: c g(n)] is an asymptotic lower bound of [MATH: f,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3014ef545bc133c22947a6f6afb9d0d5]

Content:
A related valuable concept for classifying the asymptotic behavior of algorithms is big-theta notation.

Content:
Suppose we have two nonnegative functions [MATH: f(n)] and [MATH: g(n)] such that there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] such that, for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have
[MATH: c_1 g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_2 g(n)]

Content:
as depicted in the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e5490c9a928d23acb3279bc5e0bcc1a8]

Content:
In plain English, beyond some threshold value [MATH: n_0,] the function [MATH: f(n)] is sandwiched between two multiples of [MATH: g(n),] ensuring that [MATH: f(n)] grows at the same rate as [MATH: g(n)] up to constant factors. In such cases, we write
[MATH: f(n) \in \Theta(g(n))]
where the formal definition of the set [MATH: \Theta(g(n))] is given below:
[MATH: \Theta(g(n)) = \left\{ f(n) : \exists c_1 c_2,n_0 \gt 0, \forall n \geq n_0, 0 \leq c_1g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_2 g(n)\right\}]

Content:
Big-Theta notation is helpful because it provides a tight bound on a function's growth by specifying both an upper and a lower bound.

---

Item 2 — Example: Understanding the Definition of Big-Theta

Example Prompt:
Suppose [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}.] In the context of algorithmic complexity, what is the definition of [MATH: \Theta(n^{10})?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Theta(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1,] [MATH: c_2,] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] lies between [MATH: c_1 \cdot g(n)] and [MATH: c_2 \cdot g(n).]

[MATH: \Theta(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c_1,c_2, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0\leq c_1\cdot g(n) \leq f(n) \leq c_2\cdot g(n) \big\}]

Geometrically, this means the following:

> The set [MATH: \Theta(n^{10})] consists of all the functions [MATH: f(n),] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1, c_2,] and [MATH: n_0] such that the graph of [MATH: f(n)] lies between [MATH: y=c_1\cdot n^{10}] and [MATH: y=c_2\cdot n^{10}] for all [MATH: n\geq n_0.]

Item 5 — Example: Proving That a Function Belongs to Big-Theta Set

Example Prompt:
Prove that [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2)] for [MATH: n\in\mathbb N.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Theta(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c_1], [MATH: c_2] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] lies between [MATH: c_1 \cdot g(n)] and [MATH: c_2 \cdot g(n)]

[MATH: \Theta(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c_1,c_2, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c_1\cdot g(n)\leq f(n) \leq c_2\cdot g(n) \big\}]

So, we start as shown below.

> We need to show that there exists constants [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] such that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have
> [MATH: c_1n^2 \leq 3n^2+1 \leq c_2n^2.]

Now, let's isolate [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] on the inequality.

> Dividing both sides of the inequality by [MATH: n^2,] we get follows:
> [MATH: c_{1}n^{2}|≤ 3n^{2} + 1 ≤ c_{2}n^{2}; (c_{1}n^{2})/(n^{2})|≤ (3n^{2} + 1)/(n^{2}) ≤ (c_{2}n^{2})/(n^{2}); c_{1}|≤ (3n^{2})/(n^{2}) + (1)/(n^{2}) ≤ c_{2}; c_{1}|≤ 3 + (1)/(n^{2}) ≤ c_{2}]

Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n^2} = 1] and [MATH: 3+\dfrac{1}{n^2}=4] if [MATH: n=1.] Also, [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n^2}] monotonically approach [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] That means the minimum possible value of [MATH: \left(3+\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)] is [MATH: 3] and the maximum is [MATH: 4.] As a result,
[MATH: 3\leq 3+\dfrac{1}{n^2} \leq 4]
for all [MATH: n \geq 1,] and we can now pick our constants.

> By setting [MATH: n_0=1], [MATH: c_1=3] and [MATH: c_2=4] we make the above inequality hold for any [MATH: n \geq n_0.]

Of course, other choices for the constants [MATH: c_1], [MATH: c_2,] and [MATH: n_0] may do the job, but the important thing is we found at least one such combination.

> Therefore, [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2).]

The full proof is given below.

> We need to show that there exists constants [MATH: c_1] and [MATH: c_2] such that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have
> [MATH: c_1n^2 \leq 3n^2+1 \leq c_2n^2.]
> Dividing both sides of the inequality by [MATH: n^2,] we get follows:
> [MATH: c_{1}n^{2}|≤ 3n^{2} + 1 ≤ c_{2}n^{2}; (c_{1}n^{2})/(n^{2})|≤ (3n^{2} + 1)/(n^{2}) ≤ (c_{2}n^{2})/(n^{2}); c_{1}|≤ (3n^{2})/(n^{2}) + (1)/(n^{2}) ≤ c_{2}; c_{1}|≤ 3 + (1)/(n^{2}) ≤ c_{2}]
> By setting [MATH: n_0=1], [MATH: c_1=3] and [MATH: c_2=4] we make the above inequality hold for any [MATH: n \geq n_0.]
>
> Therefore, [MATH: 3n^2+1 \in \Theta(n^2).]
